offence_severity: Minimum: Death (Section 302 of IPC carries the punishment of death or life imprisonment)
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the appellant fired three shots at the deceased, who was one of his colleagues in the Army, and this incident was witnessed by several Army personnel. The fact that the shots were fired from 8 to 10 ft was confirmed by the post-mortem examination, and the empty cartridge cases matched the weapon issued to the accused.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that the incident was witnessed by several Army personnel and that the post-mortem examination and evidence of the cartridge cases supported the findings.

legal_representation.accused: D.K. Thakur, D. Jha, Debasis Misra
legal_representation.state: P.P. Tripathi, ASG, N.S. Sweety Manchanda, Anil Katiyar, Anuj Bhandari, D.S. Mahra

appeal_history.trial_court: Convicted under Section 302 of the IPC
appeal_history.high_court: Confirmed the findings of the Court Martial

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the killing was a deliberate act of murder, as the accused fired three shots at a member of the Quick Reaction Team despite being warned, and the evidence supported the findings of the Court Martial.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the killing was an accident arising from a suspicion of a terrorist attack and that a case under Section 302 of the IPC was not made out.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that courts should not interfere with the findings of fact recorded by the Court Martial unless there is a clear error, and that the evidence must be considered as a whole.
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the Court Martial found the shooting to be a deliberate act of murder, and the High Court upheld these findings, so the Supreme Court did not interfere with the sentencing.
